summary: Alex Jaffe defines curse problems as unsolvable design problems arising when two core player promise conflict, making a perfect solution impossible. He frames curse problems as a clash between an experience (what it feels like to play) and an objective (the game's driving goal), and argues that you must sacrifice part of the fantasy to move forward. The talk provides a practical four-technique framework—Barriers, Gates, Carrots, and S'mores—to manage these curses rather than solve them outright, with applied examples from genres such as free-for-all combat, co-op play, and location-based games. Through a mix of illustrative hypotheticals (e.g., a high-skill, politics-driven fighting game) and real-game cases (No Man's Sky, Diablo III, Smash/PS All-Stars, Journey, The Sims, AlphaBear), the talk guides designers on identifying curse problems early, choosing where to sacrifice, and re-framing games so the core promises remain compelling even as the design shifts.
title: Cursed Problems in Game Design
topics: No Man's Sky promises vs reality
Diablo III auction house and commodified rewards
The Sims / AlphaBear creativity vs progression
game-state modeling (start S, objective, play space)
